methodology_full_text:
The dataset was compiled using OpenAI’s GPT‑6 Astra with Ultra reasoning, with GPT‑6 Astra Pro documented in the final research and review logs. The work comprised 16 initial research rounds, including three full-register verification exercises, followed by two further register-wide reviews and 50 additional research and review cycles. Six regional AI reviewers contributed to major assessments, with research, challenge and adjudication conducted in separate contexts of the same model. Reviewers checked whether each restriction occurred, its start and endpoint, the crossings and types of movement affected, continuity, and the reported reasons against linked source evidence. The two subsequent register-wide exercises comprised a blind reconstruction and challenge of 653 records, producing 3,918 claim assessments, and a further assessment of all 686 records and 738 phases in the expanded register. Additional chronology work assessed 519 cases and subjected 272 unresolved cases to fresh research and separate review. The final 50 cycles comprised 30 coverage-search cycles, ten targeted-verification cycles and ten audits of preselected records, providing full-record source reviews of 160 entries and addressing 176 targeted questions across 162 entries. Proposed additions were checked against existing episodes to avoid duplication, while partial reopenings and changes in restrictions were recorded as separate phases. At that stage the register contained 829 records and 1,010 phases. Automated consistency checks covered the complete final dataset; uncertain dates, source-access limitations and unresolved claims remain explicit. Those five register-wide reviews covered successive versions of the dataset; the REC50 targeted audits examined selected records.

Two additional full-register source audits then each assessed all 829 entries, using six regional AI reviewers and coordinator adjudication. Regional assignments were rotated for the second pass. Reviewers checked cited evidence and searched for missing or suspicious dates, reopening information, affected movement, exceptions and rationale attribution. The first pass made substantive corrections to 292 records; the second made further substantive corrections to 339 records and presentation-only changes to nine. Across the two passes, 505 distinct records received substantive changes. The passes added 26 and 33 phases respectively, bringing the register to 1,069 phases and 826 records with at least one included phase. The excluded road disruption and included rail suspension within SA025 remain separate. Each record received a fresh readable key-source check in the second pass; some other sources were available only as indexed extracts or remained inaccessible. Completion records an assessment, not verification of every claim. Conflicting dates, unmatched reopenings and limits on continuity remain explicit. These AI source reviews do not constitute independent human or different-model validation. The original study window ends on 21 October 2026; later checks through 26 October retain their actual evidence dates and do not backdate an onset or extrapolate closure. The current source catalogue contains 5,548 distinct recorded URLs, not a count of independent reports or successful full-text inspections.
methods: Scope

Land-border restrictions active within 21 October 2016 to 21 October 2026. Earlier starts are retained for episodes continuing into the window; reported durations are not clipped to it. One row groups an episode or regime. Each phase retains its own traffic, direction and dates.
Coverage and selection

Bounded country, period and movement searches screened leads against the full record and phase inventory. An existing episode normally received a correction or phase, rather than another parent. Negative searches do not establish that a border stayed open. Coverage is not exhaustive.
Models used

Initial research programme

Separate review contexts

Chronology follow-up

Final 50 cycles

The final 50 cycles comprised 30 coverage-search cycles, ten targeted-verification cycles and ten audits of preselected records, providing full-record source reviews of 160 entries and addressing 176 targeted questions across 162 entries.
Episodes and phases

Final catalogue
The current register has 829 records and 1,069 phases; 826 records contain at least one included phase. There are 5,548 distinct recorded source URLs.
Consistency checks
Automated consistency checks covered the complete final dataset; uncertain dates, source-access limitations and unresolved claims remain explicit.
Review coverage limits

The first five register-wide reviews covered successive versions. Two further full-register audits each assessed all 829 current entries. Assessed does not mean all attributes or dates are established.
Extent of review

The earlier 50-cycle programme added 128 records and 183 phases and included 160 full-record source reviews and 176 targeted questions across 162 parents. Subsequent full-register audits covered all 829 entries twice; review populations overlap.
Fixed source audits

Every fifth cycle used 16 parents selected before source inspection. Reviews covered occurrence and inclusion, movement and direction, every current phase and duration, rationales, source origins and geographic scope. A completed audit can retain unresolved claims; it does not certify every assertion as true.
Reading dates

Observed operation, formal policy, announced windows and intermittent regimes stay separate. A last-confirmed observation is not a reopening date. An unknown endpoint establishes neither continued closure nor reopening.
Duration units

Calendar-date differences are not measured elapsed hours. The default >24h view requires a sourced strictly-over-24-hour assessment or a defensible minimum bound. Exactly 24 hours, shorter restrictions and unestablished durations remain available under All. Policies and announced windows retain their evidence labels; duration charts require completed operational phases with supported exact dates.
Rationales and geography

Official explanations, protesters’ demands and analytical coding retain their stated attribution. Multiple supported reasons may coexist; an uncoded reason remains unknown. Each phase has its own location decision in the data companion. Unlocated phases do not inherit a parent marker or imply a whole-frontier closure.
What the URL count means

There are 5,548 distinct recorded HTTP(S) URL strings in the current per-record catalogues. Shared reports, mirrors and repeat retrievals are not independent witnesses. Recorded access can be full text, indexed extracts or unsuccessful.
Current and historical review

The latest accepted record review supplies the current label and review date. Full-record audit and targeted-question scopes are distinct. Original proposed outcomes, previous workflow labels and earlier dates remain preserved in the review history and release override audit. A completed review can leave evidence unresolved.
Country and entity filters

Country and territory filters use the reviewed named entities. Traffic-specific qualifications remain explicit, including railway-only Kaliningrad scope in EU007. Corrected country assignments do not create coordinates or imply closure at every crossing.
Sources and qualifications

The three evidence-source columns contain selected direct links. All recorded source URLs retains the complete per-record URL list, including earlier retrievals and geography references. Access labels describe recorded inspections. Read them with each phase qualification.
Using the master

Use the header filters for country/entity, research area or inclusion. Expand rows or use the formula bar for long text. The two visible worksheets are the master reader and this Methodology guide. The structured data companion retains native phases, source histories, review findings and geographic decisions.

Changes across both passes

505 distinct entries received substantive changes; the second pass also contains nine presentation-only changes. The register gained 59 phases. Unchanged records were also assessed and have source-access records.
Mixed inclusion
SA025 contributes only its documented Benapole rail-freight suspension. Its road disruption remains excluded. GL18, SUP-004 and R3-SC-004 remain wholly outside the map and analysis.

It does not establish actual completed trade that day: Telemicro reports no buying on October 11 and no exchange on October 13; Diario Libre describes the Haitian gate closed and only Dominican market activity on October 20. CC028-R1 — Longstanding restricted transport regime
Ordinary direct transport between Armenia and mainland Azerbaijan; separate Lachin and humanitarian routes excluded.
Full-blockade onset: summer 1991 (represented as 1991-06-01 to 1991-08-31); earlier interruptions were sporadic from 1989. These bounds do not date every individual road or railway closure.
Last dated general border-closure confirmation: 2025-06-12. Ordinary direct reopening is not established.
The sustained restriction exceeds 24 hours; no exact uninterrupted route-wide day total is assigned.

CC028-AUDIT20261026-1 — Longstanding restricted transport regime
Nakhchivan transport links through Armenia, distinguished from the earlier mainland blockade.
Blockade onset: June 1992 (1992-06-01 to 1992-06-30), as described by HRW. Attribution of responsibility was disputed.
Last dated general border-closure confirmation: 2025-06-12. Ordinary direct reopening is not established.
The sustained restriction exceeds 24 hours; no exact uninterrupted route-wide day total is assigned.

Current FCDO advice checked 26 October 2026 describes the Armenia–Azerbaijan border as closed. This is advisory confirmation, not a new onset or a gate-by-gate operational observation.

Security / Armed conflict and military confrontation
Interstate disputes and pressure / Diplomatic disputes and retaliation
Analytical interpretation of the conflict-associated transport blockades described by Human Rights Watch. Applies separately to CC028-R1 and CC028-AUDIT20261026-1. Responsibility for the Nakhchivan blockade was disputed: Azerbaijan attributed it to Armenia, while Armenian officials attributed the rail interruption to Azerbaijan’s blockade of Armenia. These attributed explanations do not establish the motive for every individual refusal or exceptional crossing.

CC028-R1: HRW describes sporadic Armenia-directed transport interruptions from 1989 and a full blockade by summer 1991. June–August bounds represent the reported season, not a first day for each road or railway.

CC028-AUDIT20261026-1: HRW separately dates Nakhchivan’s blockade from June 1992. The parties disputed responsibility, and the source also describes earlier train attacks; those attacks are not treated as the same continuous blockade. June bounds preserve month precision.

Both restrictions were sustained and exceed 24 hours. Their chronology must not be combined into one common 1991 onset or one exact network-wide duration. Reuters described the heavily militarised interstate border as closed on 12 June 2025; FCDO advice checked 26 October 2026 still describes closure. These general confirmations do not enumerate each route or its exceptional movements.

Armenia’s prime minister stated on 11 March 2026 that rail shipments had arrived via Azerbaijan and Georgia from November 2025, while direct regional connections remained under development. Third-country transit is not direct Armenia–Azerbaijan border reopening.

GL01-R1: Formal heavy-truck diversion effective February 28 until June 10 trial permission. RRA officially cited construction; Ugandan officials disputed this and alleged broader passenger denials. URN quotes an unnamed officer citing structural cracks, while reporting broader political allegations and travel restrictions. Political character is contested for the narrowly scoped freight measure; continuity relies on retrospective reporting and overlaps pandemic rules.

GL01-C7RWP1: The EastAfrican March 1 report describes the previous Thursday, February 28, when a Gatuna bus was allowed through after its Rwandan passengers and driver were refused; it also directly observes nationality-selective access on March 1. Construction claims do not erase the separate passenger evidence.

GL01-C7RWP2: Further dated confirmation, not proof of uninterrupted enforcement since March. August ministerial statement supports continuing advisory language, not universal denial.

GL01-C7RWP3: Last-confirmed is report date, not first relaxation. Roughly two-month retrospective description is not converted to an exact onset. Detailed anonymous interview concerns Kagitumba; introduction names Gatuna. One outlet does not establish uniform gate practice.

GL01-C7RWP5: No reverse passenger vehicle observed by the report’s 17:00 cutoff. Some passengers could not meet testing costs. National permission and this passage do not establish all-gate/group normalization; Cyanika ID travel remained restricted. Onset and continuous duration unknown.

GL01-C7RWP6: Calendar normalization of a dated relative reference, not a retrieved order. Local shopping differs from earlier passenger permission; food limits and changed testing remain. Do not extrapolate to every gate, traveler or commodity; onset and duration unknown.

phase eligibility/motive: Narrow freight-diversion phases have explicit construction/safety explanations as well as disputed political context.

onset: Passenger denial is reported for February 28 and directly observed on March 1, 2019. Earlier Ugandan official reports and the World Bank retrospective March 6 date do not establish a single first day for every gate or traffic class.

continuity: The observations do not establish one uninterrupted 2019–2022 passenger prohibition. Selective permissions existed before COVID; GL04 separately records the overlapping national health policy.

Power and regime politics / Contested governing authority

The blockade lay about two kilometres inside Serbia; alternative crossings existed. Separate Jarinje and Brnjak episodes are not joined.

Trade and protectionism / Trade and transport protests
Attributed participant demands
Polish hauliers argued that Ukrainian operators enjoyed unfair competitive advantages after permit requirements were relaxed. They sought restoration of reciprocal permit rules and changes to queue and transport-market arrangements; these are the protesters’ claims, not an independent finding of unfair competition.

These are selective commercial-freight restrictions, with changing quotas and humanitarian, military and other exceptions. Korczowa’s January 16 operational return is confirmed by the regional governor, while Ukrainian border-service accounts confirm Hrebenne and Dorohusk resumed that day. Dorohusk’s December 11 removal and December 18 restart are separate phases, supported by actual traffic during the intervening week. A truck obstructed Ukraine-bound movement December 11 evening; its cause and ending are not securely reconstructed and it does not establish uninterrupted protest. March 1 was an intended pause horizon, not the actual January reopening date. Medyka’s separate farmers’ campaign is excluded. No unchanged common three-post duration or zero-throughput claim is made.

R5-AES-003-R1 — Formal policy
Tanga regional commissioner's directive barring Kenyan truck-driver entry at Horohoro

REC50-R01-PH001 — Formal policy
Namanga Tanzanian policy statement refusing Kenyan trucks during renewed testing dispute
Start: unknown.
Last confirmed: 2020-06-03. Reciprocal permission to proceed under a new testing arrangement was reported by 2020-06-18, following the commissioner’s statement on 2020-06-17.

Health and biosecurity / Human disease control
Trade and protectionism / Customs and transport rules
Interstate disputes and pressure / Diplomatic disputes and retaliation
Reported reasons
Tanzanian officials disputed Kenya’s handling and recognition of COVID-19 tests and attributed infections to Kenyan drivers. The restrictions formed part of reciprocal testing and cargo-entry disagreements; these claims are attributed to the officials and are not independent findings about disease transmission.

Contemporary reporting distinguishes the May 17 Holili/Taveta restriction from the May 18 Tanga/Horohoro directive; no synchronized onset at every post is established. R5-AES-003-R1 retains non-Kenyan transit and cargo-transfer exceptions. May 19 is confirmation, not repeal. The May 22 bilateral testing framework is not proof of complete restoration.

REC50-R01-PH001: June 1 dates the renewed dispute; the first actual Namanga refusal remains uncertain. The indexed UNECA/WFP June 2 claim has not been upgraded into an independently verified operational onset. KNA’s June 4 spot check found no trucks crossing at that moment amid testing delays, which does not establish continuous closure. The June 18 Citizen report quotes reciprocal permission announced June 17 for crews to proceed while awaiting results. This supplies a formal-permission upper bound, not a timed operational endpoint. Its observed driver trip is into Kenya; Kenya-to-Tanzania return and the separate Horohoro reopening remain unobserved.

R6-EA-005-FU1: Dan Viet records a March 14 closure notice and a March 15 official exchange confirming clearance could not proceed.
